To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
stereo algorithms based on local matching primitives and global optimization techniques have achieved a high degree of accuracy and robustness.

stereo algorithms based on the assumption that the scene is a collection of smooth surfaces, such as those based on the epipolar constraint and on the assumption that a surface is a smooth plane, are the most accurate.

stereo matching algorithms can be divided into two broad categories, those using local matching and those using global matching; that local matching algorithms are more robust and more accurate; that global matching algorithms are faster and can handle occlusion; and that the performance of stereo algorithms is highly dependent on the type of image used.

the extraction of 3D structure information from images.
establishing stereo correspondence for extracting the 3D scene structure.
the development of a new class of stereo techniques which use a new matching primitive, namely a 2D surface patch.

stereo is still a difficult problem and there is no one algorithm that works well on all types of images.
the problem of stereo matching remains unsolved.
the stereo vision problem is far from solved.
